bivy.name: Gargett Mine basin bivy
bivy.notes: This is the base camp for American Border Peak and for the west side of Mount Larrabee, and it is what turns both from a punishing single push into a sane two-day trip. From High Pass a boot path drops north and west into the basin, reached in well under an hour from the pass and about two and a half hours from the Twin Lakes trailhead. The workings themselves sit on a bench with space for a handful of people lying down, and the friendlier option is to keep descending a few hundred feet to the green basin below, where gravel bars beside the creek take proper tents. From here the American Border Peak approach traverses Larrabee's west slope to a notch around 6,200 ft and on into the moraine bowl below the south saddle, which is the reason parties who try the peak in a day so often run out of daylight. Fill every bottle before you leave the creek. Snow lingers in the bowls above the basin all summer, and the ground is loose scree and gravel that will not hold a stake well.
bivy.water: A creek runs through the basin by the old mine, and it is the last reliable water on the way to either summit; everything beyond is snowmelt or nothing
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. No fires anywhere in the wilderness, party size twelve, pack out all waste including human waste. The old mine is an abandoned working, not a shelter; stay out of any adit. The international boundary is the other thing to have straight before you leave camp: American Border Peak's summit stands just south of it and its twin across the connecting col to the north is in another country, so on this climb the line is a route-finding constraint and not an abstraction. It is unmarked on the ground for most of its length here, there is no port of entry anywhere near, and there is no way to present yourself to either country's customs from the mountains, so crossing it, whether by carrying on along a summit ridge or dropping down the far side of a col, is an illegal entry rather than a technicality and can cost you at a staffed crossing later. Know where the line runs before you leave camp and stay south of it. This is patrolled country, so being asked for identification on the road or in the basin is routine; carry photo identification, and proof of status if you are not a citizen.
bivy.capacity: Room for only a few bivy sacks at the old mine workings themselves; several tent sites on the gravel bars in the green basin a few hundred feet lower

bivy.name: Twin Lakes Road upper section and the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead pullouts
bivy.notes: This is the road rather than a campsite, because on this approach the road is the variable that decides what the trip is. The first four and a half miles to the Tomyhoi Lake and Yellow Aster Butte trailhead are rough gravel that an ordinary car can manage with patience; the straight section below the switchbacks is the worst of it, with loose rock and deep potholes. The final two miles to Twin Lakes are narrow, unmaintained for passenger cars, short of pullouts, and genuinely want high clearance. Parties turned back at the lower lot are looking at an extra two miles and roughly 1,500 ft of road walking each way before the climb even starts, which turns a comfortable day on Winchester or a two-day Larrabee trip into something much longer, and is a good reason to plan on sleeping out. The road is snowbound well into the season most years and is often not drivable to the upper end until July. Call the ranger station before committing, and if you park low, camping in a pullout the night before is a common and reasonable way to save the morning.
bivy.water: Creeks cross the road in places but there is nothing reliable at the lot itself; carry water up from the valley or plan to filter higher
bivy.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at the trailhead, and the state parks pass is not accepted here. Fill in the free self-issue wilderness permit at the register where one is provided. Dispersed roadside camping on national forest land outside the wilderness boundary is generally allowed, but never in a way that narrows the road or blocks a pullout.
bivy.capacity: A dozen or so vehicles in the trailhead lot, plus scattered pullouts along the road; it fills on summer weekends and there is nowhere to turn around if you keep going and change your mind

bivy.name: Twin Lakes basin road-end camp
bivy.notes: This is the base for everything on the north side of the zone. An alpine cirque at 5,200 ft with the two lakes, subalpine trees and meadow, vault toilets at both lakes, picnic tables at many sites, and no drinking water. Because you can drive to it in a capable vehicle it is the only place in the zone where a heavy pack costs you nothing, so most parties on Winchester, Mount Larrabee and American Border Peak sleep here and start from the isthmus between the lakes. The Winchester Mountain trail and the High Pass trail both begin there. It does not melt out completely until July in most years, and late-season parties should expect a busy, social camp rather than a quiet one. Everything the lakes hold is heavily used; pick an established site rather than making a new one in the meadow.
bivy.water: The two lakes, right at camp. No treated water; filter or boil.
bivy.permit: Recreation pass or the posted per-vehicle day-use fee for the trailhead. Free self-issue wilderness permit at the register for anyone continuing onto the trails. The lakes basin at the road end sits outside the wilderness and several sites have metal fire rings, but everything above and beyond is wilderness where fires are prohibited outright, and county or forest-wide burn bans routinely close the road-end rings as well. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve. Hang or canister your food.
bivy.capacity: Roughly ten to fifteen informal sites spread around the two lakes; first come, first served, and competitive on any decent summer weekend

bivy.name: High Pass camp
bivy.notes: High Pass is reached from the Twin Lakes isthmus by way of the Winchester junction, a traverse under an avalanche chute, then Low Pass and a short climb, roughly two and a half miles with a little over a thousand feet of gain. It is directly on the line for both of the big objectives here: the basin north of the pass leads to the south face of Mount Larrabee and its standard south ridge scramble, and the same ground continues around Larrabee's west slope towards American Border Peak. Camping at the pass buys you height and a very short morning, and costs you water and shelter, since it is a windy notch with almost nothing flat. The snow slopes between Twin Lakes and the pass are the crux of the approach for much of the season and can stay steep and firm into August. Parties who want to sleep dry and drink freely usually pass over the top and drop into the mine basin instead.
bivy.water: Nothing running. Snow patches into midsummer are the only source, so most parties carry water from Twin Lakes or drop to the creek at the mine basin below.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Twin Lakes register. Mount Baker Wilderness rules: no fires, party size twelve, camp on durable ground, pack out all waste including human waste. The international boundary runs a little over a mile north of the pass; camp and climb south of it, and see the border note on the mine basin below.
bivy.capacity: A couple of small tent spots on and just below the pass; two or three tents at most, and they are exposed

name: Northwest Ridge
approach: Start at the Big Four Ice Caves trailhead on the Mountain Loop Highway (a Northwest Forest Pass is needed for parking). The Ice Caves trail is an easy, mostly boardwalk and paved path of about 1.1 miles each way with roughly 220 ft of gain, passing the old hotel site at the picnic area, crossing the South Fork Stillaguamish on a bridge, and opening into a meadow below the north side of the mountain. Leave the trail at the end and head across the open basin toward the foot of the north-side ridge you are climbing.

bivy.name: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac
bivy.notes: Big Four is a car-to-car objective by design: the trailhead sits at low elevation barely a mile from the base of a face that rises about 4,000 feet, so the climbing starts almost immediately and there is no approach worth camping to shorten. Parties on the north-side lines, including the long winter couloir routes, typically leave overnight gear at the base and go up and down in a push rather than carrying a bivouac onto the face, which is a considered choice on a wall this active — rockfall and avalanche off it are constant and audible through the night. That same activity is why this is a contingency and not a recommendation: sleeping under this face means sleeping under a debris cone that is there because things fall on it. Position any bivouac well out of the runout, not at the toe of the snow. The ice caves at the base are lethal and collapse every year — do not camp near them, on them, or in them, and stay off them entirely. The nearest legal drive-in beds are the developed campgrounds down the paved loop toward Verlot.
bivy.water: Creeks draining the face run all season near the base, and the debris field itself is meltwater. Treat everything. There is no developed water at the picnic area.
bivy.permit: Not inside any wilderness — this side of the highway is ordinary national forest with no camping permit requirement. A federal recreation pass is required to park at the picnic area. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer and are frequently forest-wide.
bivy.capacity: No established camp of any kind. The picnic area at the trailhead is day use only and camping there is not permitted; parties climbing the north side bivouac informally at the base of the face on the avalanche debris and boulder ground beyond the maintained path.

waypoints.name: Big Four Picnic Area / Ice Caves Trailhead

name: Northwest Couloir–North Ridge
approach: Reached via the North Fork Entiat Trail to Saska Basin and Saska Pass, commonly combined with ascents of Saska Peak, Emerald Peak, and Pinnacle Mountain on the same trip rather than as a dedicated single-peak approach. In late June the first three or four miles of the North Fork valley run through burnt forest with many fallen trees, and snow covers the trail between about 6,600 and 6,900 ft.
descent: Reverse the ridge/couloir, or descend the east/southeast slopes if that side was used to finish the climb.

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails inside the Little Giant Fire closure area (Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
bivy.notes: This is the road head for the whole eastern side of the Chelan Mountains crest and the standard place to sleep the night before a long walk in. The drive is the thing people underestimate — it is roughly 38 miles of valley road from the Columbia, most of it paved, and getting here from the west side of the state is the better part of four hours. Cottonwood sits at the end, just short of where the Entiat River trail begins. Camp here and you can be walking at first light with the entire day for the eleven miles to Entiat Meadows or the eight to Fox Camp. Recognise what has happened to this valley: successive fires have run through it and the lower trail corridor is open, burned, dusty and hot, with young growth and standing snags rather than shade. That makes the river the only dependable water for the first several miles and it makes an early start a safety measure rather than a preference. A landslide near the river trailhead currently blocks the normal approach; a temporary high-clearance route has been pushed through the slide, trailers are turned back, and the campground short of it is being used as the turnaround. Confirm before committing to the drive, because there is nothing at the end of this road.
bivy.water: The Entiat River runs beside every one of these campgrounds and is the most reliable water anywhere in the zone. Treat it. Some of the smaller road campgrounds have a hand pump but several have none at all and nothing should be assumed potable.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent recreation pass for the trailhead lot. No permit to camp. Forest-wide Stage 2 fire restrictions have prohibited campfires on all national forest land since early July 2026, including in established rings, and the county has a total outdoor burn ban. All of these campgrounds are inside the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026, and Cottonwood is written off for the remainder of the season.
bivy.capacity: Cottonwood has around two dozen sites; the string of small campgrounds down-valley adds a similar number again

bivy.name: Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp for the Chelan Mountains crest peaks. From the North Fork Entiat trailhead at roughly 3,880 ft the trail runs about eight miles to the Pyramid trail junction, with Fox Camp a quarter mile north of it. Every one of Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain is reachable from here, which is what makes this the single most useful site here — a party that carries in once can pick off several summits over consecutive days rather than repeating the approach. Saska is the shortest of them, essentially a scramble off the trail near where it crosses the south ridge at Saska Pass; Emerald and Cardinal need the higher basin above. Note this is a different spur road and a different trailhead from the Entiat River trail at the end of the valley, and the two are easy to confuse when planning — turn off roughly 35 miles up rather than driving to the road's end. Season is July through early October, though the larch in late September is the standout. The valley is dry and hot low down and the camp is a genuine relief after it.
bivy.water: The North Fork Entiat River is beside the trail for most of the approach and there is water at the camp. It holds through the season in a normal year. Above Fox Camp the Pyramid trail climbs onto drier ground where water becomes intermittent snowmelt only, so this is the last certain fill for parties going high.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue at the trailhead register, party limit of twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the North Fork Entiat trailhead. No campfires under the current forest-wide Stage 2 restrictions. The North Fork Entiat River and Pyramid trails are both named in the current fire closure order through 31 October 2026.
bivy.capacity: An established backcountry camp with room for a couple of parties; the sites along this trail are described as roomy

name: East Face
approach: Shares the same remote, multi-day approach as the peak's northwest-couloir route: via Hannegan Pass Trail and Whatcom/Perfect Pass to the Challenger Glacier and West Challenger Notch, descending to a camp on the Crooked Thumb Glacier below the peak's north/east side (or via the alternate Big Beaver Trailhead-Wiley Ridge-Challenger Arm approach).
descent: not recorded; presumed to reverse the east face or descend via the adjacent northwest-couloir line back to the glacier.

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. Walk-up only and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp
bivy.notes: Narrow lateral moraine at the southern edge of the Crooked Thumb Glacier, reached from Perfect Pass across the Challenger Glacier and down through the notch west of Challenger. The base camp for Crooked Thumb and Phantom from the north. Fully exposed to weather.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and glacier melt only
bivy.permit: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone)
bivy.capacity: A few tents on a narrow moraine

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. Whatcom Camp and both Graybeal camps have been closed because of fire damage from 2022, and the park's fire-closures page, updated September 14, 2026, still lists them closed until further notice, so there is no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as closed for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
bivy.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
bivy.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
bivy.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste must be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

waypoints.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass

name: Standup Creek Route
approach: Access is via Standup Creek Road, reached from Stafford Creek Road off the Teanaway River Road near Cle Elum. The Standup Creek Trail #1369 follows an old road with little early elevation gain, crosses Standup Creek six to seven times, passes through brushy sections with some downed trees, then switchbacks up through forest and meadows to the ~6,200-ft saddle at the head of the drainage. The Labor Mountain Fire closure order on this trail has been lifted, as the Cle Elum Ranger District's trail crew reported on September 25, 2026; expect burned forest and downed trees in the drainage.
descent: Most parties either retrace the Standup Creek Trail or descend via the Southwest Ridge/Bean Creek Trail as a loop (requires a car shuttle or road walk between trailheads).

name: Tahoma Cleaver
approach: From Westside Road — Dry Creek Trailhead, walk the closed road past the barricade to the Tahoma Creek Trail and climb it about 2 miles to the Wonderland Trail junction near 4300 ft. Go south over the Tahoma Creek suspension bridge, follow the Wonderland Trail to Indian Henry's Hunting Ground, then take the Mirror Lakes Trail until it fades in the basin between Copper and Pyramid Peaks. Continue cross-country past Pyramid Peak to Success Cleaver and climb it to about 8000 ft, where glacier travel begins. A roped traverse across the South Tahoma Glacier at roughly 8100 ft reaches the base of Tahoma Cleaver.

name: Avalanche-White Salmon Glaciers
approach: Start at the Cold Springs trailhead (about 5,600 ft) at the end of FR 8040 and walk the South Climb Trail up the old roadbed to its junction with the Round the Mountain Trail near 6,200 ft. Turn right (northwest) onto the Round the Mountain Trail and follow its up-and-down traverse for roughly two miles, much of it under snow in early season, to the stream draining the Avalanche Glacier basin near 6,100 ft. Follow the stream and the moraines above it to the moraine-filled bowl at about 7,200 ft, where the Avalanche Glacier route and the Southwest Chutes meet. The glacier begins above this bowl, and a camp here shortens the summit day.

name: Mazama Glacier Headwall
approach: Start from the Bird Creek Road trailhead (~5,700 ft) on the Yakama Reservation side; route-finding across moraines and glacier fields begins around 6,700 ft, reaching Sunrise Camp at 8,300 ft. The Yakama Nation decides each year whether overnight stays are allowed, so plan a single-day push in day-use-only years.
descent: Reverse the ascent: back down the glacier past Sunrise Camp and out the way you came in to Bird Creek Meadows. Descending the South Spur instead is possible, but it is not a variation on the same day out - it finishes at the Cold Springs / South Climb trailhead on the mountain's south side, reached by an entirely different road system from the Yakama Nation approach this route starts on, so it only works if you have a vehicle waiting there. A party that walks off south without one has left its car on the far side of the mountain.

bivy.name: Sunrise Camp

name: Pinnacle Glacier Headwall
approach: A free wilderness permit is self-issued at the trailhead. From the Riley Camp Trailhead, hike the Riley Camp Trail, staying off the Riley Cut-Off at the first junction, until it meets the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn south on the Pacific Crest Trail for a few minutes to Riley Creek and follow the creek up through boulders to the moraines at the foot of the Pinnacle Glacier. The headwall route begins at the base of the glacier.

name: Coleman Ski Descent
approach: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (about 3,700 ft) at the end of Glacier Creek Road (FR 39) and follow Trail 677 through old growth, crossing several creeks that run higher in the afternoon than the morning. At about two miles and 4,700 ft you pass the former Kulshan Cabin site, then a signed junction: the left fork goes to the Coleman Glacier overlook and the right fork is the climbers' trail. Take the climbers' trail steeply up the Hogsback moraine ridge to the edge of the Coleman Glacier near 6,000 ft, where most parties camp. In winter and spring the road may be gated miles short of the trailhead, which adds distance, and the glacier is skinned from there toward the Deming.

name: Squak Glacier
approach: From the Park Butte/Schriebers Meadow trailhead area, take the Scott Paul Trail; around 4,600 ft leave the maintained trail for the climbers' path to Crag View camp (~6,500 ft, about 3.5 mi from the trailhead with roughly 3,300 ft of gain).
descent: Descend via the Squak Glacier and Roman Wall back to Crag View Camp using the approach route in reverse. Total descent 3-4 hours.

bivy.name: Crag View Camp

name: Southwest Route
approach:
Crowder has no trail and no road anywhere near it, and the way in is from the north, down the west side of the Picket Range. From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead, walk over Hannegan Pass and down to the Chilliwack River, ford it, and climb onto Easy Ridge. Follow the ridge over Easy Peak, get around the Imperfect Impasse gap (in most years by dropping well below it and climbing back up an exposed class 4 step) and carry on to Perfect Pass. From there keep heading south across the western slopes of the range, below Challenger, Crooked Thumb and Ghost Peak, to the west side of Phantom Peak, then continue south to the col between Phantom and Crowder, at a little over 6,000 ft, where the climb starts. Allow at least two days to reach the col.

The other way in comes from the west and is seldom used: the Baker River Trail, then the high route along Pioneer Ridge, whose southeast end sits at the bottom of Crowder's easy southwest slopes.
descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

bivy.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
bivy.notes: Open ground above 6,000 ft on the crest of Easy Ridge, near Easy Peak (6,615 ft), where an old fire lookout once stood. It is the end of the first long day from the trailhead: over Hannegan Pass, down to the Chilliwack River, across it and up the ridge. The next morning starts with the detour around the Imperfect Impasse, a drop of several hundred feet and a climb back up, before Perfect Pass.
bivy.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
bivy.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
bivy.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. Walk-up only and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier moraine camp
bivy.notes: A moraine camp at the southern edge of the Crooked Thumb Glacier, below Ghost Peak, on the west side of the range. It is reached from Perfect Pass across the Challenger Glacier, and it is the last camp on record before the Phantom-Crowder col, which lies further south along the west side of Phantom Peak. Fully exposed to weather.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and glacier melt only
bivy.permit: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone)
bivy.capacity: A few tents on a narrow moraine

waypoints.name: Chilliwack River ford / Easy Ridge climbers' path
Col between Phantom Peak and Crowder

name: Lynch Glacier
approach: From the Deception Pass Trailhead, hike to Marmot/Jade Lakes, continue to Dip Top Gap, then traverse west to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage and descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.
descent: Reverse the ascent: back down the glacier (finger or Class 3 bypass depending on season), over Dip Top Gap, past Marmot/Jade Lakes, to the Deception Pass Trailhead.

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond, below Cathedral Rock
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Daniel and the eastern option for Mount Hinman, and by a distance the most convenient high camp on this side of the divide. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac roughly eleven to twelve miles of rough, narrow gravel to the Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end, take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up to the pass near 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft directly under Cathedral Rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly step that is a genuine obstacle for some parties under an overnight pack. From the pond the standard Daniel route takes the southeast ridge between Circle Lake and the permanent snowfield to the saddle below the east summit at about 7,899 ft and on to the true summit at 7,959 ft, the highest point in the Alpine Lakes; the Lynch Glacier on the north side is the historic line and has shrunk sharply in recent years, draining into Pea Soup Lake. Hinman from here is the less direct half of its two approaches — it means traversing the northeast slopes of Daniel at around 5,300 ft to Pea Soup Lake, crossing to its west end, dropping to about 5,500 ft and then climbing southwest to the summit — long, and much easier under continuous snow than on late-season talus. The Necklace Valley side is the shorter way to Hinman; come here when Daniel is the objective, or when you want both. The critical 2026 caveat: the Cle Elum River road and the Cathedral Pass trail have been inside a fire-area closure running from mid-August to the end of October, along with the campgrounds along that road, so the entire eastern approach has been shut for the back half of the season. Confirm the closure has lifted before driving out — it is a four-hour round trip from the Foss side to find out the hard way.
bivy.water: The pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it, reliable through the normal season. Squaw Lake, about 800 ft lower on the trail in, is the fallback and the overflow camp.
bivy.permit: This is the most restricted camp in the zone and the rules are the point. Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Campfires are prohibited outright — the pond is well above the fire-ban line, the basin is fragile and badly worn, and there is no wood. Party size is reduced here: plan on eight rather than the usual twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group that size. Camp only on the existing hardened pads; areas posted as closed for restoration are legally off limits and staying in one is a violation, not a discourtesy. Do not build wind blocks or fire rings — this is the single most common damage in the basin. Move on rock rather than heather. The spur trail is hiker-only, so no stock.
bivy.capacity: Small and strictly limited. Roughly four or five levelled bivouac pads plus a marginal sloping one, and several of the larger areas that used to be camped have been flagged for restoration and are closed. It fills, and there is no honest overflow inside the basin.

bivy.name: Hyas Lake and Upper Hyas Lake
bivy.notes: The low-effort basecamp on the Cle Elum side, less than two miles up the Deception Pass trail from the Tucquala Meadows road end on a gentle grade through meadow and forest, sitting at about 3,471 ft with Cathedral Rock and the Daniel massif standing over it. For Mount Daniel it is the family-friendly alternative to Peggy's Pond and it is honest to say what that costs: camping here rather than at the pond adds roughly two thousand feet to summit day and puts the whole approach to the southeast ridge in front of you before the climbing starts. It earns its place for three reasons — it is the fallback when Peggy's Pond is full, which it often is; it is the sensible choice for a party larger than the pond's reduced limit allows; and it is by far the better place to sit out weather, being sheltered, wooded and low. The valley floor around Fish Lake and Tucquala Lake below the trailhead also holds dispersed and developed camping if you arrive late and want to walk in fresh. Two caveats. Mosquitoes here are serious from snowmelt through midsummer, worse than at the pond. And the same fire-area closure applies as at Peggy's Pond — the Cle Elum River road, the Deception Pass trail and the campgrounds along the road were all shut from mid-August to the end of October in 2026, so this entire approach depends on that closure having lifted.
bivy.water: The lakes and the Cle Elum River flowing through them. Reliable all season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Party size twelve. Camp at the established sites and keep back from the shoreline — a 200 ft setback applies at listed lakes on this side of the range. Check the current campfire order before lighting anything; at this elevation a fire may be legal when the district is not under a seasonal ban, but the sites nearest the water are heavily worn and a stove is the better choice regardless.
bivy.capacity: Plenty. Established sites and a privy along the shores of both lakes, spread out enough that even a busy weekend does not feel packed. This is the one place in the zone where a large party can settle without a problem.

name: Southeast Chute
approach: Two trailheads serve this climb. The Upper Trailhead (about 3,500 ft, at the end of the short spur off Forest Road 2419, pass required) is the usual start from roughly June through October, once the road has melted out. From about December into May the road is commonly blocked by snow at or just past the Lower Trailhead (about 2,600 ft, no pass needed), so winter and spring parties park there and add roughly 1,000 ft of climbing and a few miles to the day; in heavy snow even that lot can be out of reach and a party may have to begin at the Big Creek campground gate. The trail from the lower lot meets the one from the upper lot near 3,900 ft, so everything above is the same. Continue to the signed junction near 4,500 ft where the winter route leaves the summer trail and heads right into the basin below the chute.

name: West Ridge
approach: Park at the Necklace Valley (East Fork Foss) trailhead at the end of FR 68 and follow the East Fork Foss trail up the valley. The first five miles are gentle forest, gaining only about 600 ft, until a footlog crossing of the East Fork Foss River, then the trail climbs about 2,400 ft in three miles of steep, rooty switchbacks to Jade Lake and on up the Necklace Valley past the other lakes. Leave the valley trail at its upper end, where the hanging valley leads to La Bohn Lakes and the climb proper. Camps at the lakes or in Necklace Valley make this a two-day trip for most parties. From the end of the valley, hug the tree line left, following cairns up heather to the outlet of the lower La Bohn Lake, then continue to the upper lake; the ridge above it is the start of the climb.

name: The Hexorcist
approach: No maintained trail reaches the north face. Parties generally leave the West Ridge boot path or approach cross-country from the Anderson Creek drainage / FR 6220 area, bushwhacking through steep second-growth and old-growth timber to gain the base of the wall; expect substantial off-trail forest travel and real route-finding difficulty.
descent: Not documented for this specific route; likely descends via the peak's easier west-ridge/back-side terrain, as is typical for north-face routes on this peak, but this is not confirmed anywhere.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

name: Bloody Head Couloir
approach: Drive to Ruth Creek Road's end at Hannegan Campground via Mt. Baker Hwy (SR 542) and Hannegan Pass Road (FS 32)/Ruth Creek Road. From the Ruth Creek trail at about 3,450 ft, leave the trail, drop southwest to cross Ruth Creek, and cross talus to the base of the couloir at about 4,000 ft.

bivy.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
bivy.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.
bivy.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
bivy.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends

waypoints.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road

name: White Salmon Glacier
approach: From the small pull-off at the old White Salmon Lodge on the Mount Baker Highway, walk around the gate and follow the old road past the lodge site for about a mile to where it ends at an old clearcut. With good snow cover, descend northeast to White Salmon Creek and follow the valley up to the toe of the White Salmon Glacier. Without it, hold your height through the clearcut and contour, losing elevation only to get around rock bands and stream crossings, to stay out of the slide alder in the valley bottom. Bivy sites sit among the rock outcrops along the eastern edge of the glacier.
descent: Reverse the route; it is the most common descent for northside Shuksan climbs (North Face, Northeast Ridge, Hanging Glacier).

bivy.name: Rock outcrop bivy, east edge of the lower White Salmon Glacier
bivy.notes: Bivy on the rock outcrops along the eastern edge of the White Salmon Glacier near its foot. Camp here rather than in the approach valley, which is under icefall from the Hanging Glacier.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and glacial runoff
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit
bivy.capacity: Small flat spots among rock outcrops; a few tents

bivy.name: Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
bivy.notes: Camping above the chimneys is what makes Fisher Chimneys a comfortable two- or three-day climb rather than a very long push, and it puts the party above the loose, route-finding-heavy section for summit day. The lower site near the top of the White Salmon is the more common choice and the more scenic; the higher one above Winnie's Slide costs you a steep snow or ice pitch with a full pack. Which is preferable depends on the party and on conditions in the chimneys, and reasonable people disagree. Both are small and exposed, so a party arriving to find them occupied needs a plan.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only in practice. Runoff sometimes appears on the rock below the glaciers in warm conditions, but neither site should be planned around finding liquid water.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — these camps are inside the park, past the signed boundary above Lake Ann. Reserve through Recreation.gov or take a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center within 24 hours; fees apply and the zone carries a small daily party quota. A Northwest Forest Pass covers only the parking at the Lake Ann trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Small platforms for one or two parties at each of two levels — around 6,800 ft where the chimneys top out near the White Salmon, and higher near 7,300 ft above Winnie's Slide

waypoints.name: White Salmon Lodge road gate (Mount Baker Highway hairpin)

name: Mount Si Trail
approach: From Seattle, take I-90 east to Exit 32 (436th Ave SE). Turn left and go north on 436th Ave SE to its end at SE North Bend Way. Turn left, and after 0.3 mi turn right onto SE Mt. Si Road. Follow it 2.4 mi to the large trailhead lot on the left. The trail starts at the lot. Keep left at the Talus Loop junction at about 0.7 mi, and continue past Snag Flats (about 2 mi) to Haystack Basin (about 4 mi).
descent: Return the way you came on the same trail.

name: First Divide Route (North Fork Skokomish / Staircase approach)
approach: From the Staircase trailhead area on the North Fork Skokomish River, follow the North Fork Skokomish River Trail 12.7 miles to First Divide (elevation about 4,688 ft), passing through lowland and montane forest into subalpine meadow with views of the La Crosse Peaks. From First Divide, continue cross-country to reach Mount Steel's summit. In August, the full day from Staircase to the summit and back is roughly 29 miles with around 7,000 ft of gain, so it is a very long single push or an overnight at the lower camps.
descent: Reverse the route back to First Divide and down the North Fork Skokomish Trail to Staircase.

bivy.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
bivy.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.
bivy.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. Campfires are prohibited, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
bivy.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads

bivy.name: Camp Pleasant — mid-valley staging on the North Fork Skokomish
bivy.notes: About 6.2 to 6.7 miles up the valley at low elevation, this is the standard first night for a First Divide trip and the obvious place to stop if you started driving late. It serves none of the Sawtooth peaks directly — the Flapjack junction is well behind you by here — but it breaks the long walk to Steel, Hopper and the Upper Duckabush into sensible pieces. From Camp Pleasant it is under three miles on to Nine Stream and about six and a half on to Home Sweet Home. Old-growth forest, deep shade, mosquitoes in early summer, and no views to speak of. Usable most of the year when the road is open, which makes it a genuine shoulder-season option in a zone where everything higher is under snow.
bivy.water: Reliable year round — the North Fork Skokomish runs beside the camp
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. This is not a quota camp, so it is generally available at short notice. Bear canisters are required. It sits below 3,500 ft, so campfires are allowed in the established rings using dead and down wood, subject to the seasonal bans that are usually in force from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A roomy forested riverside camp with several sites, a privy and a bear wire; one of the more comfortable valley camps and it seldom fills

bivy.name: Nine Stream — last low camp before the First Divide climb
bivy.notes: At roughly 9.6 miles and just over 2,000 ft, this is where the valley trail stops being flat. Everything above it climbs hard to First Divide at about 4,690 ft. Its specific value is Mount Hopper: the Hopper way trail leaves the main trail around the 12.4 mile mark, and a party camped at Nine Stream can reach it and be on the summit and back in a long day without carrying over the divide. It is also the last sensible water-and-shelter stop for anyone pushing through to Home Sweet Home in one go from the trailhead, which is a 13-mile day most people do not want with a climbing pack. Buggy in early summer and gloomy, but sheltered, and the low elevation means it stays usable when the divide is still buried.
bivy.water: Reliable — the river and the side stream the camp is named for
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, booked through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp. Bear canisters are required. Below the 3,500 ft line, so fires are permitted in the established rings when no seasonal ban is in effect.
bivy.capacity: Several sites among the trees near the creek confluence, with a privy; usually quiet

waypoints.name: Staircase Trailhead (North Fork Skokomish, Olympic NP)
Camp Pleasant — mid-valley staging on the North Fork Skokomish
Nine Stream — last low camp before the First Divide climb

name: Happy Creek Route
approach: In deep winter, park at the SR 20 closure gate (typically near the Ross Dam Trailhead) and walk/ski the closed highway to the Happy Creek area. In spring, when WSDOT has plowed several additional miles toward Happy Creek, park at the Happy Creek Nature Trail lot directly. In mid-March of a low-snow year the highway walk was part bare and the trail was snow-free up to the first meadow; skins went on near 3,300 ft, with logs, rocks and alder to dodge between about 3,000 and 4,000 ft. By late May the lower creek corridor turns into dense alder and devil's club above ~4,300 ft; continuous snow begins near 4,700 ft. A narrow break in the cliffs near 5,100 ft leads to the open upper slopes.
descent: Descend the same Happy Creek drainage line back to the highway.

waypoints.name: Happy Creek trailhead (Happy Creek Forest Walk lot, SR 20)

name: Northwest Ridge Route
approach: From Newhalem, drive or walk SR 20 east about 12 miles (0.4 mi west of Horsetail Creek, ~2.8 mi northeast of Colonial Creek Campground) to a turnout at about 1,900 ft elevation, directly across from a large boulder field on Ruby's northwest side.
descent: Descend the same northwest/west ridge line back to the highway turnout.

name: Squak Glacier Route
approach: Approach from the Schriebers Meadow Trailhead (~3,366 ft) as for the Easton Glacier route, branching onto the Squak Glacier line rather than the Railroad Grade/Easton line; high camp is commonly established around 6,500 ft. In early June the Scott Paul trail is the usual way up to about 4,700 ft before joining the glacier line; camp at Crag View is near 6,100 ft.
descent: Descend via the ascent route, or via a ski/downclimb line around the bergschrund hazard zone when conditions allow.

bivy.name: Crag View, Squak Glacier
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Sherman Peak's Squak Glacier route and it is the site the Mount Baker file does not cover, since everything written there is on the Easton or the Coleman. It sits about 3.5 miles and 3,300 ft above Schriebers Meadow: the Park Butte trail past Sulphur Creek and the meadows, then a climbers' path leaving the trail around 4,600 ft and running up onto the moraine. From here the route makes a rising traverse of the Squak toward Sherman's south ridge, roughly 3,600 ft to the summit. The Squak is an early-season objective and the reason is specific — a bergschrund opens across the line as the season goes on and can shut the route down entirely by late summer, so a July plan is a different proposition from a May one. The lower part of the approach is outside the wilderness and carries snowmobile traffic into early July. Forest Road 13 off Road 12 is gravel and holds snow late; check it before a long drive.
bivy.water: No potable water at the trailhead or anywhere on the route. Melt channels run near the moraine edge in early summer and are gone or unreliable by August, so plan on melting snow and carry the fuel for it.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit, but camping below 6,000 ft on this route is prohibited, which is the practical reason Crag View exists where it does. A recreation pass is required to park at the Park Butte trailhead. Party size is capped at 12 once you enter the wilderness, campfires are prohibited, and there is no toilet anywhere on the route — carry blue bags, which are handed out free at the ranger offices in Sedro-Woolley and at Glacier. Nothing may be buried in snow or dropped into a crevasse or moat.
bivy.capacity: The established climbers' camp on the Squak, with room for several parties on gravel benches and snow platforms at the toe of the glacier; quieter than the Easton side even on a summer weekend

bivy.name: Upper Squak benches, Sulphur moraine and the rock prow
bivy.notes: Parties who want Sherman's summit day short move above Crag View and camp on the Sulphur moraine at the glacier's edge around 7,000 ft, or push on to the flatter ground below the rock prow closer to 7,600 ft. The gain is real, since it takes a good chunk out of the traverse to the south ridge and puts you at the base of the steep snow with the night's freeze still holding. The cost is a fully exposed camp on a volcano's south flank, where wind is the usual reason parties come back down to Crag View, and you are already on glacier and roped to get here. Camping this high also means committing to melt water, which drives fuel weight up. Where exactly the platforms are usable moves year to year with the crevasse pattern, so arrive with daylight to scout rather than in the dark.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow. Anything running here in early summer is a bonus and will not be there later in the year.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness rules as at Crag View — no permit to camp, recreation pass at the Park Butte trailhead, 12-person party limit, no campfires, all waste packed out in blue bags.
bivy.capacity: Dug snow platforms and moraine gravel for one or two parties along the right-hand edge of the glacier, with a second bench under a rock prow several hundred feet higher; no established sites and no shelter
